newsitem.title: USA: Colombia rebuts McCaffrey charges on drug kings.
newsitem.headline: Colombia rebuts McCaffrey charges on drug kings.

text.p: Colombia's foreign minister responded angrily in a letter made public on Wednesday to criticisms by White House drug czar Barry McCaffrey of lenient sentences passed on former leaders of the Cali drug cartel.

The minister, Maria Emma Mejia, voiced "extreme disappointment and concern" at McCaffrey's comments on Sunday on the jail terms handed down last Friday on billionaire cocaine kings Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela.

In a letter to McCaffrey dated Tuesday and circulated on Wednesday by the Colombian embassy in Washington, Mejia said her government shared U.S. outrage at the light terms and resented implications it had connived in the sentencing.

The Rodriguez Orejuela brothers received sentences that would see them walk free in five years. They were granted maximum sentence reductions by a Colombian judge after admitting their role in creating a worldwide criminal empire and smuggling tons of cocaine into the United States.
McCaffrey said in a statement the "artificial sentences ... demonstrate the urgent need for Colombia to pass sentencing reform legislation as soon as possible".
But Mejia described McCaffrey's comments as "counter-productive to our efforts in the difficult struggle against drugs and narco-traffickers".

She said it was well known to the U.S. government the brothers had been sentenced under laws in effect in 1994 for crimes committed before that date and could not have been punished under any stiffer laws passed subsequently.

"I am disappointed that a situation of which both governments were aware ... has been used as a weapon to gain an advantage in a publicity campaign which will only serve to make cooperation between our governments more difficult," she said.
Mejia said "no one was more outraged" at the sentences than Colombian President Ernesto Samper and his administration.

"It therefore saddened me greatly to read your recent comments suggesting that this administration had somehow played a role in the sentencing of the Rodriguez Orejuela brothers," Mejia told McCaffrey.
At stake is whether Colombia will regain "certification" this year as a U.S. ally in the war against drugs in an annual report due out in March.
Amid allegations Samper's election campaign had benefited from drug money, Colombia lost certification last year, and with it most U.S. aid.
